title: Des Teufels rußiger Bruder
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 100. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 100, a soldier’s bargain-with-the-devil tale that pairs neatly with the one after it in this batch. A discharged soldier with nothing to live on hires himself to the devil for seven years — tending the fires under hell’s cauldrons, forbidden to wash, comb, or trim his nails — and is sent home with a knapsack of sweepings that turns to gold once he is above ground again, along with the sooty title that follows him. Filthy, ragged and frightening to look at, he still talks his way into an inn and, eventually, into marrying a king’s youngest daughter, the only one of three willing to have him out of duty to her father.

sentences.t: Ein abgedankter Soldat hatte nichts zu leben und wußte sich nicht mehr zu helfen.
sentences.l: A discharged soldier had nothing to live on and knew no more how to help himself.
sentences.i: A discharged soldier had nothing to live on and was at his wits’ end.
sentences.n: abgedankt is dismissed from service, paid off — the soldier turned loose after a war, a familiar figure in these tales. “sich nicht zu helfen wissen” is to be at the end of one’s resources.

sentences.t: Da gieng er hinaus in den Wald, und als er ein Weilchen gegangen war, begegnete ihm ein kleines Männchen, das war aber der Teufel.
sentences.l: Then went he out into the wood, and when he had gone a little while, a little man met him, but that was the devil.
sentences.i: So he went out into the forest, and when he had walked a while a little man met him — but that was the devil.
sentences.n: gieng is the 1857 spelling of ging. begegnen takes the dative of the person met, ihm. Männchen is the diminutive of Mann and neuter, so the das that follows refers to it. The tale says who he is at once and leaves the soldier to find out.

sentences.t: Das Männchen sagte zu ihm „was fehlt dir? du siehst ja so trübselig aus.“
sentences.l: The little man said to him “what is wanting to you? you look so woebegone.”
sentences.i: The little man said to him: “What ails you? You look so woebegone.”
sentences.n: “was fehlt dir?” is the everyday “what is the matter with you?” — what is lacking to you, with the person in the dative. aussehen is separable, “siehst … aus.” ja is the particle, appealing to what is plain to see.

sentences.t: Da sprach der Soldat „ich habe Hunger aber kein Geld.“
sentences.l: Then said the soldier “I have hunger but no money.”
sentences.i: Then the soldier said: “I am hungry, but I have no money.”
sentences.n: German has hunger rather than being hungry — Hunger haben. sprach for “said” runs through all these tales.

sentences.t: Der Teufel sagte „willst du dich bei mir vermiethen und mein Knecht sein, so sollst du für dein Lebtag genug haben;
sentences.l: The devil said “will you hire yourself out to me and be my servant, then shall you have enough for your lifetime;
sentences.i: The devil said: “If you will hire yourself out to me and be my servant, you shall have enough for your lifetime;
sentences.n: A conditional with no wenn: “willst du dich … vermiethen,” with the verb first, does the work of “if you will.” sich vermiethen, modern vermieten, is to hire oneself out as a servant. Der Lebtag is one’s living days, all one’s life. Ein Knecht is a farm-servant, a hired man.

sentences.t: sieben Jahre sollst du mir dienen, hernach bist du wieder frei.
sentences.l: seven years shall you serve me, thereafter are you free again.
sentences.i: you shall serve me seven years, and after that you are free again.
sentences.n: dienen takes the dative, mir. hernach is the older “after that.” Seven years is the standing term of service in these tales, and it is kept to the day.

sentences.t: Aber eins sag ich dir, du darfst dich nicht waschen, nicht kämmen, nicht schnippen, keine Nägel und Haare abschneiden und kein Wasser aus den Augen wischen.“
sentences.l: But one thing tell I you, you must not wash yourself, not comb yourself, not snip, cut no nails and hair and wipe no water out of the eyes.”
sentences.i: But one thing I tell you: you must not wash, nor comb yourself, nor blow your nose, nor cut your nails and hair, nor wipe the water out of your eyes.”
sentences.n: dürfen with a negative is not “may not” but “must not.” schnippen is to snap the fingers, and of the nose to clear it with a snap of them — the countryman’s way, and that is most likely what is forbidden here, though the reading is not quite certain. Not wiping his eyes means they will run and go bleary, which is the look he is to carry out of hell.

sentences.t: Der Soldat sprach „frisch dran, wenns nicht anders sein kann,“ und gieng mit dem Männchen fort, das führte ihn geradewegs in die Hölle hinein.
sentences.l: The soldier said “briskly at it, if it cannot be otherwise,” and went off with the little man, which led him straight into hell.
sentences.i: The soldier said: “At it then, if it can be no otherwise,” and went off with the little man, who led him straight down into hell.
sentences.n: “frisch dran” is the soldier’s own idiom — fresh at it, in with a will. wenns = wenn es. geradewegs is straight, by the direct road, and “in die Hölle hinein” doubles the direction with hinein, right in.

sentences.t: Dann sagte es ihm was er zu thun hätte:
sentences.l: Then told it him what he had to do:
sentences.i: Then he told him what he was to do:
sentences.n: es, it, stands for the little man, because Männchen is neuter. thun is the 1857 tun. “was er zu thun hätte,” with the subjunctive, is what he was to do, in reported speech.

sentences.t: er müßte das Feuer schüren unter den Kesseln, wo die Höllenbraten drin säßen, das Haus rein halten, den Kehrdreck hinter die Thüre tragen, und überall auf Ordnung sehen:
sentences.l: he must poke the fire under the kettles, where the hell-roasts sat inside, keep the house clean, carry the sweepings behind the door, and see everywhere to order:
sentences.i: he was to poke the fire under the cauldrons where the roasts of hell sat inside, keep the house clean, carry the sweepings behind the door, and see to order everywhere.
sentences.n: Höllenbraten is a compound made for the joke — the roasting meat of hell, meaning the souls in the pots. Der Kehrdreck is the dirt swept up, from kehren, to sweep; carrying it behind the door instead of out of the house is odd housekeeping, and the tale will make something of that. Thüre keeps the 1857 th. The verbs stay in the subjunctive of reported speech.

sentences.t: aber guckte er ein einziges Mal in die Kessel hinein, so würde es ihm schlimm ergehen.
sentences.l: but peeped he a single time into the kettles, then would it go badly for him.
sentences.i: but if he peeped into the cauldrons a single time, it would go badly with him.
sentences.n: Another conditional with no wenn — “guckte er … hinein,” with the verb first, is “if he peeped.” “es ergeht jemandem schlimm” is the impersonal “it goes badly with someone.”

sentences.t: Der Soldat sprach „es ist gut, ich wills schon besorgen.“
sentences.l: The soldier said “it is good, I will see to it right enough.”
sentences.i: The soldier said: “Very well, I shall see to it.”
sentences.n: wills = will es. besorgen is to see to a thing, to take care of it; schon is again the particle of confidence, never fear.

sentences.t: Da gieng nun der alte Teufel wieder hinaus auf seine Wanderung, und der Soldat trat seinen Dienst an, legte Feuer zu, kehrte und trug den Kehrdreck hinter die Thüre, alles wie es befohlen war.
sentences.l: Then went now the old devil out again on his wandering, and the soldier entered on his service, laid fire on, swept and carried the sweepings behind the door, all as it was commanded.
sentences.i: Then the old devil went out again on his travels, and the soldier entered on his service: he laid on the fire, swept, and carried the sweepings behind the door, all as he had been told.
sentences.n: antreten and zulegen are both separable and both stand split — “trat … an,” “legte … zu.” “einen Dienst antreten” is to enter on a service; “Feuer zulegen” is to lay more fuel on.

sentences.t: Wie der alte Teufel wieder kam, sah er nach ob alles geschehen war, zeigte sich zufrieden und gieng zum zweitenmal fort.
sentences.l: When the old devil came again, looked he to see whether everything had been done, showed himself satisfied and went off for the second time.
sentences.i: When the old devil came back he looked to see whether all had been done, showed himself satisfied, and went off a second time.
sentences.n: nachsehen, separable, is to look into a thing, to check it. zum zweitenmal is for the second time, printed here as one word.

sentences.t: Der Soldat schaute sich nun einmal recht um, da standen die Kessel rings herum in der Hölle, und war ein gewaltiges Feuer darunter, und es kochte und brutzelte darin.
sentences.l: The soldier looked about him now properly for once, there stood the kettles round about in hell, and was a mighty fire under them, and it boiled and sizzled inside.
sentences.i: Now the soldier had a good look about him: the cauldrons stood all round about in hell, with a mighty fire under them, and inside there was a boiling and a sizzling.
sentences.n: sich umschauen is separable and reflexive, to look about one. brutzeln is the word for the noise of fat in a pan, to sizzle and splutter — a kitchen word set down in hell. The es of “und war ein gewaltiges Feuer” is left out; German drops it once the sentence is under way.

sentences.t: Er hätte für sein Leben gerne hinein geschaut, wenn es ihm der Teufel nicht so streng verboten hätte:
sentences.l: He would for his life gladly have looked in, if the devil had not forbidden it him so strictly:
sentences.i: He would have given his life to look in, if the devil had not forbidden it so strictly.
sentences.n: “für sein Leben gern” is a fixed phrase — to want a thing more than anything, for one’s life. verbieten takes the dative of the person, ihm.

sentences.t: endlich konnte er sich nicht mehr anhalten, hob vom ersten Kessel ein klein bischen den Deckel auf und guckte hinein.
sentences.l: at last could he hold himself back no more, lifted from the first kettle the lid a little bit up and peeped in.
sentences.i: At last he could hold out no longer; he lifted the lid of the first cauldron a little way and peeped in.
sentences.n: sich anhalten is to hold oneself in, to restrain oneself. aufheben is separable — “hob … auf.” bischen is the 1857 spelling of bißchen.

sentences.t: Da sah er seinen ehemaligen Unteroffizier darin sitzen:
sentences.l: There saw he his former sergeant sitting in it:
sentences.i: There he saw his former sergeant sitting in it.
sentences.n: Ein Unteroffizier is a non-commissioned officer, the man who had the soldier under him; the three in the pots — sergeant, ensign, general — are his old superiors, and they come in rising order.

sentences.t: „aha, Vogel,“ sprach er, „treff ich dich hier? du hast mich gehabt, jetzt hab ich dich,“ ließ geschwind den Deckel fallen, schürte das Feuer und legte noch frisch zu.
sentences.l: “aha, bird,” said he, “do I meet you here? you have had me, now have I you,” let the lid fall quickly, poked the fire and laid on fresh besides.
sentences.i: “Aha, my bird,” said he, “do I find you here? You had me once; now I have you” — and he let the lid drop smartly, poked up the fire and laid on more fuel.
sentences.n: Vogel as a form of address is mocking — you fine bird, you rogue. “du hast mich gehabt” is to have had someone under one, to have had the whip hand; the soldier’s whole revenge sits in the change of tense. “noch frisch zulegen” is to lay on more fresh fuel.

sentences.t: Danach gieng er zum zweiten Kessel, hob ihn auch ein wenig auf und guckte, da saß sein Fähnrich darin:
sentences.l: After that went he to the second kettle, lifted it too a little up and looked, there sat his ensign in it:
sentences.i: After that he went to the second cauldron, lifted it a little too and looked, and there sat his ensign.
sentences.n: Ein Fähnrich is the ensign, the officer who carried the flag — die Fahne — the lowest commissioned rank. In “hob ihn … auf” the ihn is the lid, understood from the sentence before, though the German lets it stand for the kettle.

sentences.t: „aha, Vogel, treff ich dich hier? du hast mich gehabt, jetzt hab ich dich,“ machte den Deckel wieder zu und trug noch einen Klotz herbei, der sollte ihm erst recht heiß machen.
sentences.l: “aha, bird, do I meet you here? you have had me, now have I you,” made the lid fast again and carried another block over, that should make it right hot for him.
sentences.i: “Aha, my bird, do I find you here? You had me once; now I have you” — and he shut the lid again and fetched another log, which was to make it good and hot for him.
sentences.n: The same words a second time, and a third to come; the tale gives him one speech and lets him say it over each of his old officers. zumachen and herbeitragen are separable and both stand split. “erst recht” is properly, all the more so.

sentences.t: Nun wollte er auch sehen wer im dritten Kessel säße, da wars gar ein General:
sentences.l: Now wanted he to see also who might be sitting in the third kettle, there it was actually a general:
sentences.i: Now he wanted to see who was sitting in the third cauldron too — and there it was a general, no less.
sentences.n: säße is the subjunctive after an indirect question. gar here is the intensifying “actually, no less,” not “not at all.” wars = war es.

sentences.t: „aha, Vogel, treff ich dich hier? du hast mich gehabt, jetzt hab ich dich,“ holte den Blasbalg und ließ das Höllenfeuer recht unter ihm flackern.
sentences.l: “aha, bird, do I meet you here? you have had me, now have I you,” fetched the bellows and let the hell-fire flare up properly under him.
sentences.i: “Aha, my bird, do I find you here? You had me once; now I have you” — and he fetched the bellows and made the fire of hell blaze up under him in earnest.
sentences.n: Der Blasbalg is the bellows, the blowing-bag. lassen with an infinitive — “ließ … flackern” — is to make a thing happen, here to make the flames leap.

sentences.t: Also that er sieben Jahr seinen Dienst in der Hölle, wusch sich nicht, kämmte sich nicht, schnippte sich nicht, schnitt sich die Nägel und Haare nicht und wischte sich kein Wasser aus den Augen;
sentences.l: So did he seven years his service in hell, washed himself not, combed himself not, snipped himself not, cut himself the nails and hair not and wiped himself no water out of the eyes;
sentences.i: So he did his seven years’ service in hell: he did not wash, did not comb himself, did not blow his nose, did not cut his nails and hair, and wiped no water from his eyes.
sentences.n: that is the 1857 spelling of tat. The whole list of prohibitions comes back word for word as a list of things done — or rather not done, which is the tale’s way of paying out seven years in a single sentence. “schnitt sich die Nägel” is the dative of possession: the person in the dative, the nails with a plain article.

sentences.t: und die sieben Jahre waren ihm so kurz, daß er meinte es wäre nur ein halbes Jahr gewesen.
sentences.l: and the seven years were so short to him, that he thought it had been only half a year.
sentences.i: and the seven years seemed so short to him that he thought it had been only half a year.
sentences.n: “sie waren ihm kurz” — the dative of the person for whom they were short. “wäre … gewesen” is the subjunctive of reported thought.

sentences.t: Als nun die Zeit vollends herum war, kam der Teufel und sagte „nun, Hans, was hast du gemacht?“
sentences.l: When now the time was quite round, came the devil and said “now, Hans, what have you done?”
sentences.i: When the time was fully up, the devil came and said: “Well, Hans, what have you been doing?”
sentences.n: “die Zeit ist herum” — the time is up, gone round. The soldier is called Hans here for the first time; Hans is the name for any man in these tales, as Jack is in English, and he keeps it to the end.

sentences.t: „Ich habe das Feuer unter den Kesseln geschürt, ich habe gekehrt und den Kehrdreck hinter die Thüre getragen.“
sentences.l: “I have poked the fire under the kettles, I have swept and carried the sweepings behind the door.”
sentences.i: “I have poked the fire under the cauldrons, I have swept and carried the sweepings behind the door.”
sentences.n: He answers in the devil’s own words from the first day, and leaves out the one thing he also did.

sentences.t: „Aber du hast auch in die Kessel geguckt;
sentences.l: “But you have also peeped into the kettles;
sentences.i: “But you did peep into the cauldrons;
sentences.n: The devil knows it without being told; nothing in his house goes unseen.

sentences.t: dein Glück ist, daß du noch Holz zugelegt hast, sonst war dein Leben verloren;
sentences.l: your luck is, that you laid on more wood, otherwise was your life lost;
sentences.i: your luck is that you laid on more wood, or else your life was forfeit;
sentences.n: “dein Glück ist, daß …” — it is your good fortune that. The plain past war stands where modern German would put wäre gewesen: otherwise your life would have been lost.

sentences.t: jetzt ist deine Zeit herum, willst du wieder heim?“
sentences.l: now is your time round, do you want to go home again?”
sentences.i: now your time is up — will you go home again?”
sentences.n: “wieder heim” with no verb of motion: German lets the verb of going drop when the direction says it.

sentences.t: „Ja,“ sagte der Soldat, „ich wollt auch gerne sehen was mein Vater daheim macht.“
sentences.l: “Yes,” said the soldier, “I would also gladly see what my father is doing at home.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” said the soldier, “I should like to see what my father is doing at home.”
sentences.n: wollt is the clipped wollte, here a wish — I should like. daheim is at home, where heim is homeward.

sentences.t: Sprach der Teufel „damit du deinen verdienten Lohn kriegst, geh und raffe dir deinen Ranzen voll Kehrdreck und nimms mit nach Haus.
sentences.l: Said the devil “so that you get your earned wages, go and rake yourself your knapsack full of sweepings and take it with you home.
sentences.i: The devil said: “So that you get the wages you have earned, go and rake your knapsack full of sweepings and take it home with you.
sentences.n: raffen is to rake or scrape a thing together with both hands. “raffe dir” is the dative of interest, rake yourself full. Ein Ranzen is the knapsack a soldier carries on his back. nimms = nimm es.

sentences.t: Du sollst auch gehen ungewaschen und ungekämmt, mit langen Haaren am Kopf und am Bart, mit ungeschnittenen Nägeln und mit trüben Augen, und wenn du gefragt wirst, woher du kämst, sollst du sagen „aus der Hölle“, und wenn du gefragt wirst, wer du wärst, sollst du sagen „des Teufels rußiger Bruder, und mein König auch.“
sentences.l: You shall also go unwashed and uncombed, with long hairs on the head and on the beard, with uncut nails and with bleary eyes, and if you are asked, from where you came, shall you say ‘out of hell’, and if you are asked, who you were, shall you say ‘the devil’s sooty brother, and my King as well’.”
sentences.i: You shall go unwashed and uncombed too, with long hair on your head and in your beard, with uncut nails and bleary eyes; and when you are asked where you come from, you shall say ‘out of hell’, and when you are asked who you are, you shall say ‘the devil’s sooty brother, and my King besides’.”
sentences.n: trüb of eyes is clouded, bleary. kämst and wärst are the subjunctive of reported speech inside the devil’s instruction. The answer he is given is the tale’s title: rußig is sooty, from der Ruß, soot, and “und mein König auch” claims the devil for his king as well as his brother — a boast and a blasphemy both, and he says it to every innkeeper he meets. The 1857 text sets its quotation inside the quotation with the same marks, and lets one closing mark serve for both.

sentences.t: Der Soldat schwieg still und that was der Teufel sagte, aber er war mit seinem Lohn gar nicht zufrieden.
sentences.l: The soldier kept quite silent and did what the devil said, but he was not at all satisfied with his wages.
sentences.i: The soldier held his peace and did what the devil said, but he was not at all satisfied with his wages.
sentences.n: “still schweigen” doubles the silence — to keep quite quiet. “gar nicht” is not at all, which is what gar means beside a negative.

sentences.t: Sobald er nun wieder oben im Wald war, hob er seinen Ranzen vom Rücken und wollt ihn ausschütten:
sentences.l: As soon as he was now up in the wood again, lifted he his knapsack from his back and wanted to shake it out:
sentences.i: As soon as he was up in the forest again he lifted the knapsack from his back and made to shake it out.
sentences.n: oben, above, because hell is below and the wood is at the top of the way he came. ausschütten is separable, to tip a thing out.

sentences.t: wie er ihn aber öffnete, so war der Kehrdreck pures Gold geworden.
sentences.l: but when he opened it, so had the sweepings become pure gold.
sentences.i: But when he opened it, the sweepings had turned to pure gold.
sentences.n: The sweepings he was told to carry behind the door, and not out of the house, are the wages after all — the tale has kept that quiet since the first page. The so before the main clause is the old resumptive “then.”

sentences.t: „Das hätte ich mir nicht gedacht“ sprach er, war vergnügt und gieng in die Stadt hinein.
sentences.l: “That should I not have thought” said he, was content and went into the town.
sentences.i: “I should never have thought it,” said he; and he was well pleased, and went on into the town.
sentences.n: “sich etwas denken” is to imagine a thing to oneself, with the dative mir. There is no comma before sprach — 1857 punctuation around speech is looser than ours.

sentences.t: Vor dem Wirthshaus stand der Wirth, und wie ihn der heran kommen sah, erschrack er, weil Hans so entsetzlich aussah, ärger als eine Vogelscheuche.
sentences.l: Before the inn stood the innkeeper, and when he saw him coming up, he took fright, because Hans looked so dreadful, worse than a scarecrow.
sentences.i: The innkeeper was standing in front of his inn, and when he saw him coming up he took fright, for Hans looked so dreadful, worse than a scarecrow.
sentences.n: Wirthshaus and Wirth keep the 1857 th (modern Wirtshaus, Wirt). erschrack is the old past of erschrecken, modern erschrak. ärger is the comparative of arg, worse; eine Vogelscheuche is the bird-scare, the scarecrow.

sentences.t: Er rief ihn an und fragte „woher kommst du?“ „Aus der Hölle.“
sentences.l: He called out to him and asked “where do you come from?” “Out of hell.”
sentences.i: He called out to him and asked: “Where do you come from?” “Out of hell.”
sentences.n: anrufen, separable, is to call out to someone, to hail him. The answer is the devil’s, word for word as he was told to give it, and the tale sets it down with no speech tag at all.

sentences.t: „Wer bist du?“ „Dem Teufel sein rußiger Bruder, und mein König auch.“
sentences.l: “Who are you?” “The devil his sooty brother, and my King as well.”
sentences.i: “Who are you?” “The devil’s sooty brother, and my King besides.”
sentences.n: “dem Teufel sein Bruder” is the possessive built with a dative and a following pronoun — the devil his brother — which is how ordinary speech owns a thing where the written language says des Teufels, as the tale’s title does.

sentences.t: Nun wollte der Wirth ihn nicht einlassen, wie er ihm aber das Gold zeigte, gieng er und klinkte selber die Thüre auf.
sentences.l: Now would the innkeeper not let him in, but when he showed him the gold, went he and unlatched the door himself.
sentences.i: The innkeeper would not let him in; but when Hans showed him the gold, he went and unlatched the door himself.
sentences.n: einlassen and aufklinken are both separable. Die Klinke is the latch of a door, so aufklinken is to lift the latch and open it — done by the innkeeper’s own hand, which is the measure of what gold does.

sentences.t: Da ließ sich Hans die beste Stube geben und köstlich aufwarten, aß und trank sich satt, wusch sich aber nicht und kämmte sich nicht, wie ihm der Teufel geheißen hatte, und legte sich endlich schlafen.
sentences.l: Then had Hans the best room given him and himself waited on splendidly, ate and drank himself full, but washed himself not and combed himself not, as the devil had bidden him, and laid himself at last to sleep.
sentences.i: Then Hans had the best room given him and was waited on splendidly, ate and drank his fill, but did not wash and did not comb himself, as the devil had bidden him, and at last lay down to sleep.
sentences.n: “sich geben lassen” is to have a thing given one, to order it. aufwarten is to wait at table. “sich satt essen” is to eat oneself full. heißen here is to bid, to command, not to be called.

sentences.t: Dem Wirth aber stand der Ranzen voll Gold vor Augen und ließ ihm keine Ruhe, bis er in der Nacht hinschlich und ihn wegstahl.
sentences.l: To the innkeeper however the knapsack full of gold stood before the eyes and let him no rest, until he crept there in the night and stole it away.
sentences.i: But the knapsack full of gold stood before the innkeeper’s eyes and let him have no rest, until in the night he crept over and stole it away.
sentences.n: “jemandem vor Augen stehen” is to stand before someone’s eyes, to haunt him; the dative dem Wirth names the man and the eyes take a plain article. hinschleichen and wegstehlen are separable and both stand split.

sentences.t: Wie nun Hans am andern Morgen aufstand, den Wirth bezahlen und weiter gehen wollte, da war sein Ranzen weg.
sentences.l: When now Hans got up the next morning, wanted to pay the innkeeper and go on further, then was his knapsack gone.
sentences.i: When Hans got up the next morning, meaning to pay the innkeeper and go on his way, his knapsack was gone.
sentences.n: “am andern Morgen” is the next morning, ander in its old sense of second, following. aufstehen is separable; weg is simply away, gone.

sentences.t: Er faßte sich aber kurz, dachte „du bist ohne Schuld unglücklich gewesen,“ und kehrte wieder um, geradezu in die Hölle:
sentences.l: He took it however shortly, thought “you have been unlucky without fault of your own,” and turned back again, straight into hell:
sentences.i: But he made short work of it, thought: “You have come to grief through no fault of your own,” and turned back, straight to hell.
sentences.n: “sich kurz fassen” is to be brief, to make short work of a thing. He speaks to himself as du, which German does freely. umkehren is separable — “kehrte … um.” geradezu is straight, directly.

sentences.t: da klagte er dem alten Teufel seine Noth und bat ihn um Hülfe.
sentences.l: there complained he to the old devil his distress and asked him for help.
sentences.i: There he told the old devil his trouble and asked him for help.
sentences.n: “jemandem seine Noth klagen” is a fixed old phrase — to pour out one’s trouble to someone. Noth and Hülfe keep the 1857 spellings (modern Not, Hilfe).

sentences.t: Der Teufel sagte „setze dich, ich will dich waschen, kämmen, schnippen, die Haare und Nägel schneiden und die Augen auswischen,“ und als er mit ihm fertig war, gab er ihm den Ranzen wieder voll Kehrdreck und sprach „geh hin, und sage dem Wirth er sollte dir dein Gold wieder herausgeben, sonst wollt ich kommen und ihn abholen, und er sollte an deinem Platz das Feuer schüren.“
sentences.l: The devil said “sit yourself down, I will wash you, comb you, snip you, cut the hair and nails and wipe out the eyes,” and when he was finished with him, gave he him the knapsack full of sweepings again and said “go there, and tell the innkeeper he should give you back your gold, otherwise would I come and fetch him away, and he should poke the fire in your place.”
sentences.i: The devil said: “Sit down, I will wash you, comb you, blow your nose, cut your hair and nails and wipe out your eyes”; and when he had finished with him he gave him the knapsack full of sweepings again, and said: “Go, and tell the innkeeper he is to give you back your gold, or else I will come and fetch him away, and he shall poke the fire in your place.”
sentences.n: Everything forbidden for seven years is done for him now in a single line, and in the very order in which it was forbidden. sollte and wollt are the subjunctive of the devil’s reported threat. abholen, separable, is to come and fetch someone away — said of the devil, it needs no explaining.

sentences.t: Hans gieng hinauf und sprach zum Wirth „du hast mein Gold gestohlen, gibst dus nicht wieder, so kommst du in die Hölle an meinen Platz, und sollst aussehen so gräulich wie ich.“
sentences.l: Hans went up and said to the innkeeper “you have stolen my gold, give you it not back, then come you into hell in my place, and shall look as horrible as I.”
sentences.i: Hans went up and said to the innkeeper: “You have stolen my gold; if you do not give it back, you will go to hell in my place and shall look as horrible as I do.”
sentences.n: hinauf, up, because hell is below. “gibst dus nicht wieder” is a conditional with the verb first and no wenn — if you do not give it back; dus = du es. gräulich is horrible, frightful.

sentences.t: Da gab ihm der Wirth das Gold und noch mehr dazu, und bat ihn nur still davon zu sein;
sentences.l: Then gave him the innkeeper the gold and more besides, and begged him only to be quiet about it;
sentences.i: Then the innkeeper gave him the gold and more besides, and begged him only to say nothing of it.
sentences.n: “still davon sein” is to keep quiet about a thing. nur softens the demand into a plea.

sentences.t: und Hans war nun ein reicher Mann.
sentences.l: and Hans was now a rich man.
sentences.n: The clause stands alone after the semicolon, and the tale is content to say it plainly and leave it.

sentences.t: Hans machte sich auf den Weg heim zu seinem Vater, kaufte sich einen schlechten Linnenkittel auf den Leib, gieng herum und machte Musik, denn das hatte er bei dem Teufel in der Hölle gelernt.
sentences.l: Hans made himself on the way home to his father, bought himself a poor linen smock onto his body, went about and made music, for that had he learned with the devil in hell.
sentences.i: Hans set out on the road home to his father, bought himself a coarse linen smock to wear, and went about making music, for that he had learned from the devil in hell.
sentences.n: “sich auf den Weg machen” is to set out. schlecht here is plain, poor in quality, its older sense; ein Kittel is a smock or frock worn over the clothes, and “auf den Leib kaufen” is bought onto the body, to wear.

sentences.t: Es war aber ein alter König im Land, vor dem mußt er spielen, und der gerieth darüber in solche Freude, daß er dem Hans seine älteste Tochter zur Ehe versprach.
sentences.l: But there was an old King in the land, before whom he had to play, and he fell over it into such joy, that he promised Hans his eldest daughter in marriage.
sentences.i: But there was an old King in the land before whom he had to play, and the King fell into such delight over it that he promised Hans his eldest daughter in marriage.
sentences.n: mußt is the clipped mußte. “in Freude gerathen” is to fall into joy — the same verb that puts a man into a deep sleep or into misfortune elsewhere. “zur Ehe versprechen” is to promise in marriage.

sentences.t: Als die aber hörte daß sie so einen gemeinen Kerl im weißen Kittel heirathen sollte, sprach sie „eh ich das thät, wollt ich lieber ins tiefste Wasser gehen.“
sentences.l: But when she heard that she was to marry so common a fellow in the white smock, she said “before I did that, would I rather go into the deepest water.”
sentences.i: But when she heard that she was to marry so common a fellow in a white smock, she said: “Before I did that, I would sooner go into the deepest water.”
sentences.n: die at the head of the clause is the demonstrative — she, the eldest daughter. gemein in 1857 is common, low-born, without the modern sense of nasty. thät is the subjunctive of thun (modern täte). To go into the deepest water is to drown oneself, said plainly and left there.

sentences.t: Da gab ihm der König die jüngste, die wollts ihrem Vater zu Liebe gerne thun;
sentences.l: Then gave him the King the youngest, she would gladly do it for her father’s sake;
sentences.i: Then the King gave him the youngest, who was willing to do it for her father’s sake.
sentences.n: wollts = wollte es. “jemandem zu Liebe” is for someone’s sake, out of love for them. The tale does not ask what she thought of the sooty brother.

sentences.t: und also bekam des Teufels rußiger Bruder die Königstochter und als der alte König gestorben war auch das ganze Reich.
sentences.l: and so got the devil’s sooty brother the King’s daughter and, when the old King had died, the whole kingdom as well.
sentences.i: and so the devil’s sooty brother got the King’s daughter, and when the old King had died, the whole kingdom as well.
sentences.n: The title comes back for the last line: the man is never named at the end, only called by the boast the devil put in his mouth. des Teufels is the written genitive standing before its noun, where the innkeeper heard the spoken “dem Teufel sein.”

glossary.alter: alt — old (adj., nom. sg. masc.; ein alter König)
glossary.anhalten: sich anhalten — to hold oneself back, to restrain oneself
glossary.aufstand: aufstehen — got up, rose (3rd sg. past; separable: stand auf)
glossary.darüber: darüber — at that, over that (gerieth darüber in Freude)
glossary.drin: drin — in there, inside (colloquial for darin)
glossary.eins: eins — one thing (neuter pronoun; eins sag ich dir)
glossary.ergehen: ergehen — to fare, to go for someone (impersonal: es ergeht ihm schlimm)
glossary.erst: erst — in „erst recht“: properly, all the more so
glossary.es: es — it, and 'he' of das Männchen (neuter); also the impersonal es
glossary.faßte: sich kurz fassen — made short work of it, was brief (faßte sich kurz)
glossary.gar: gar — actually, no less (intensifier: gar ein General); with a negative, gar nicht: not at all
glossary.hab: haben — (I) have (1st sg. present, clipped habe)
glossary.hob: heben — lifted (3rd sg. past; with auf: aufheben, to lift up)
glossary.hölle: die Hölle — hell (noun, f.; the place itself)
glossary.ja: ja — yes; also the particle: after all, you see
glossary.kehrte: kehren — swept (kehrte und trug den Kehrdreck); with um: umkehren, turned back
glossary.klagte: klagen — poured out, complained of (+ dat. of the person: jemandem seine Noth klagen)
glossary.leben: leben — to live, to live on (infinitive; nichts zu leben haben)
glossary.macht: machen — does, is doing (3rd sg. present; was mein Vater macht)
glossary.mußt: müssen — had to (3rd sg. past, clipped mußte)
glossary.sag: sagen — (I) tell, say (1st sg. present, clipped sage)
glossary.sage: sagen — say! tell! (imperative sg.; not die Sage, legend)
glossary.schlechten: schlecht — plain, poor in quality (older sense; ein schlechter Kittel, a coarse smock)
glossary.schon: schon — right enough, never fear (particle of confidence); also already
glossary.setze: sich setzen — sit down! (imperative sg.: setze dich)
glossary.siehst: aussehen — (you) look, appear (2nd sg.; separable: siehst … aus)
glossary.trat: antreten — entered on (his service) (3rd sg. past; separable: trat … an)
glossary.wollt: wollen — wanted, would (clipped wollte, 1st and 3rd sg.)
glossary.ärger: arg — worse (comparative of arg; ärger als eine Vogelscheuche — not der Ärger)
